claim: Animals and humans have a remarkable ability to adapt their learning rate according to the volatility of the environment.
source: Recent experiments have shown that animals and humans have a remarkable ability to adapt their learning rate according to the volatility of the environment.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from recent experiments in the abstract.

claim: The neural mechanism responsible for adaptive learning has remained unclear.
source: Yet the neural mechanism responsible for such adaptive learning has remained unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: A metaplastic synaptic model within a decision-making network can capture a wide range of key experimental findings.
source: We found that our model, which assumes that synaptic plasticity is guided by a novel surprise detection system, captures a wide range of key experimental findings and performs as well as a Bayes optimal model, with remarkably little parameter tuning.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the authors' modeling work.

claim: The metaplastic synaptic model performs as well as a Bayes optimal model with remarkably little parameter tuning.
source: We found that our model, which assumes that synaptic plasticity is guided by a novel surprise detection system, captures a wide range of key experimental findings and performs as well as a Bayes optimal model, with remarkably little parameter tuning.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract comparing model performance.

claim: Adaptation takes place over a wide range of timescales, with temporal dynamics often captured by power-law or collection of multiple exponents rather than a single exponent.
source: From neurons to behavior, evidence shows that adaptation takes place over a wide range of timescales, with temporal dynamics often captured by power-law, or collection of multiple exponents, rather than a single exponent (Thorson and Biederman-Thorson, 1974; Ulanovsky et al., 2004; Corrado et al., 2005; Fusi et al., 2007; Kording et al., 2007; Wark et al., 2009; Lundstrom et al., 2010; Rauch et al., 2003; Pozzorini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous experimental and theoretical work.

claim: Single-exponent model analysis of behavioral data showed that the time constant of exponents (or learning rate) changed across trials.
source: On the other hand, single-exponent model analysis of behavioral data showed that the time constant of exponents (or learning rate) changed across trials (Behrens et al., 2007; Rushworth and Behrens, 2008; Soltani et al., 2006; Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012; Neiman and Loewenstein, 2013; McGuire et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Activity-dependent synaptic plasticity plays a crucial role in learning and adaptation in general.
source: While theoretical and experimental studies strongly suggest that activity-dependent synaptic plasticity plays a crucial role in learning and adaptation in general (Martin et al., 2000; Kandel et al., 2000; Dayan and Abbott, 2001), the neural mechanisms behind flexible learning, especially in the case of decision making under uncertainty, has remained unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: The neural mechanisms behind flexible learning in decision making under uncertainty has remained unclear.
source: While theoretical and experimental studies strongly suggest that activity-dependent synaptic plasticity plays a crucial role in learning and adaptation in general (Martin et al., 2000; Kandel et al., 2000; Dayan and Abbott, 2001), the neural mechanisms behind flexible learning, especially in the case of decision making under uncertainty, has remained unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Standard learning models which use a single learning rate fail to capture multiple timescales of adaptation.
source: Standard learning models which use a single learning rate, α, fail to capture multiple timescales of adaptation, including those described by a power-law, since these models can only store and update memory on a single timescale of τ∼1/α.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of standard models based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: Single learning rate models can only store and update memory on a single timescale of τ∼1/α.
source: Standard learning models which use a single learning rate, α, fail to capture multiple timescales of adaptation, including those described by a power-law, since these models can only store and update memory on a single timescale of τ∼1/α.
evidence: This is a theoretical property of single learning rate models.

claim: The transition rate α of switch-like synaptic models effectively functions as the learning rate of systems with populations of such synapses in a decision making network.
source: It has been shown that its transition rate α effectively functions as the learning rate of systems with populations of such synapses in a decision making network (Soltani and Wang, 2006; Fusi et al., 2007; Iigaya and Fusi, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: The plausible assumption of bounded synapses fails to capture key phenomena of adaptive learning, including well-documented multiple timescales of adaptation.
source: However, by itself, the plausible assumption of bounded synapses fails to capture key phenomena of adaptive learning, including well-documented multiple timescales of adaptation (Thorson and Biederman-Thorson, 1974; Ulanovsky et al., 2004; Corrado et al., 2005; Fusi et al., 2007; Kording et al., 2007; Wark et al., 2009; Lundstrom et al., 2010; Rauch et al., 2003; Pozzorini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation with citations to experimental findings.

claim: There are various chemical cascade processes taking place in synapses that affect synaptic plasticity.
source: It is however known that there are various chemical cascade processes taking place in synapses that affect synaptic plasticity (Citri and Malenka, 2008; Kotaleski and Blackwell, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chemical cascade processes in synapses operate on a wide range of timescales.
source: Those processes, in general, operate on a wide range of timescales (Zhang et al., 2012; Kramar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cascade model of synapses can efficiently capture the widely-observed power-law forgetting curve.
source: The resulting model can efficiently capture the widely-observed power-law forgetting curve (Wixted and Ebbesen, 1991).
evidence: This is stated as a property of the cascade model with citation to experimental observation.

claim: Application of the cascade model has been limited to studies of the general memory storage problem.
source: However, application has been limited to studies of the general memory storage problem (Fusi et al., 2005; Savin et al., 2014), where synapses passively undergo transitions in response to uncorrelated learning events.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation with citations to previous work.

claim: Humans and other animals have a remarkable ability to actively adapt themselves to changing environments.
source: Indeed, recent experiments show that humans and other animals have a remarkable ability to actively adapt themselves to changing environments.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from recent experiments.

claim: Animals can react rapidly to abrupt step-like changes in environments.
source: For instance, animals can react rapidly to abrupt step-like changes in environments (Behrens et al., 2007; Rushworth and Behrens, 2008; Soltani et al., 2006; Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012; Neiman and Loewenstein, 2013; McGuire et al., 2014), or change their strategies dynamically (Summerfield et al., 2011; Donoso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Animals can change their strategies dynamically.
source: For instance, animals can react rapidly to abrupt step-like changes in environments (Behrens et al., 2007; Rushworth and Behrens, 2008; Soltani et al., 2006; Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012; Neiman and Loewenstein, 2013; McGuire et al., 2014), or change their strategies dynamically (Summerfield et al., 2011; Donoso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The original cascade model is likely to be able to naturally encode multiple timescales of reward information.
source: While the original cascade model (Fusi et al., 2005) is likely to be able to naturally encode multiple timescales of reward information (Corrado et al., 2005; Fusi et al., 2007; Bernacchia et al., 2011; Iigaya et al., 2013; Iigaya, 2013), such active adaptation may also require external guidance, such as in the form of a surprise signal (Hayden et al., 2011; Garvert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a likely property with citations to previous work.

claim: Active adaptation may require external guidance, such as in the form of a surprise signal.
source: While the original cascade model (Fusi et al., 2005) is likely to be able to naturally encode multiple timescales of reward information (Corrado et al., 2005; Fusi et al., 2007; Bernacchia et al., 2011; Iigaya et al., 2013; Iigaya, 2013), such active adaptation may also require external guidance, such as in the form of a surprise signal (Hayden et al., 2011; Garvert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citations to relevant work.

claim: Computational studies of changes in learning rates have largely been limited to optimal Bayesian inference models.
source: So far the computational studies of such changes in learning rates have largely been limited to optimal Bayesian inference models (e.g. Behrens et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous computational work with citation.

claim: Bayesian models provide limited insight into how probabilistic inference can be implemented in neural circuits.
source: While those models can account for normative aspects of animal's inference and learning, they provide limited insight into how probabilistic inference can be implemented in neural circuits.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of Bayesian models.

claim: The cascade model of synapses can capture the remarkable flexibility shown by animals in changing environments, but under the condition that synaptic plasticity is guided by a novel surprise detection system.
source: Our primary finding is that the cascade model of synapses can indeed capture the remarkable flexibility shown by animals in changing environments, but under the condition that synaptic plasticity is guided by a novel surprise detection system with simple, non-cascade type synapses.
evidence: This is stated as the primary finding of the study.

claim: The cascade model of synapses is able to consolidate reward information in a stable environment.
source: In particular, we show that while the cascade model of synapses is able to consolidate reward information in a stable environment, it is severely limited in its ability to adapt to a sudden change in the environment.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work.

claim: The cascade model is severely limited in its ability to adapt to a sudden change in the environment.
source: In particular, we show that while the cascade model of synapses is able to consolidate reward information in a stable environment, it is severely limited in its ability to adapt to a sudden change in the environment.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work.

claim: The surprise detection system can detect abrupt changes in the environment and facilitate adaptation by enhancing the synaptic plasticity of the decision-making network.
source: The addition of a surprise detection system, which is able to detect such abrupt changes, facilitates adaptation by enhancing the synaptic plasticity of the decision-making network.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work.

claim: The model can capture spontaneous recovery of preference.
source: We also shows that our model can capture other aspects of learning, such as spontaneous recovery of preference (Mazur, 1996; Gallistel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with citations to experimental phenomena.

claim: Animals show probabilistic choices described by the matching law in concurrent variable interval schedules.
source: Although the optimal behavior is to repeat a deterministic choice sequence according to the contingencies, animals instead show probabilistic choices described by the matching law (Herrnstein, 1961; Sugrue et al., 2004; Lau and Glimcher, 2005) in which the fraction of choices is proportional to the fraction of rewards obtained from the choice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The best probabilistic behavior under concurrent VI schedule is to throw a dice with a bias given by the matching law.
source: In fact, the best probabilistic behavior under this schedule is to throw a dice with a bias given by the matching law (Sakai and Fukai, 2008; Iigaya and Fusi, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The decision-making network has been previously shown to produce the matching law.
source: We therefore assume that the goal of subjects in this case is to implement the matching law, which has previously been shown to be produced by the model under study (Soltani and Wang, 2006; Fusi et al., 2007; Wang, 2008; Iigaya and Fusi, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: The decision-making network shows attractor dynamics with bi-stability, corresponding to a winner-take-all process acting between action selection populations.
source: It has been shown that this network shows attractor dynamics with bi-stability, corresponding to a winner-take-all process acting between action selection populations.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of the network model.

claim: The decision probability can be well approximated by a sigmoid of the difference between the strength of two synaptic populations EA and EB.
source: It has been shown that the decision probability can be well approximated by a sigmoid of the difference between the strength of two synaptic populations EA and EB (Soltani and Wang, 2006):
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous modeling work.

claim: A high rate of synaptic plasticity is necessary to react to a sudden change, but at the cost of very noisy estimation.
source: This is due to the trade-off: a high rate of synaptic plasticity is necessary to react to a sudden change, but at the cost of very noisy estimation (as the synapses inevitably track local noise).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical property demonstrated in the model.

claim: The choice probability is reliable only if the rate of plasticity is set to be very small (α=0.002); however, then the system cannot adjust to a rapid unexpected change in the environment.
source: As seen in Figure 1B,C, the choice probability is reliable only if the rate of plasticity is set to be very small (α=0.002); however, then the system cannot adjust to a rapid unexpected change in the environment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Highly plastic synapses (α=0.2) can react to a rapid change, but with a price to pay as a noisy estimate afterwards.
source: On the other hand, highly plastic synapses (α=0.2) can react to a rapid change, but with a price to pay as a noisy estimate afterwards (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Experimental studies suggest that animals integrate reward history on multiple timescales rather than a single timescale.
source: Experimental studies suggest that they integrate reward history on multiple timescales rather than a single timescale (Corrado et al., 2005; Fusi et al., 2007; Bernacchia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Animals can change the integration timescale, or the learning rate, depending on the environment.
source: Other studies show that animals can change the integration timescale, or the learning rate, depending on the environment (Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In the cascade model, the degree of synaptic strength is assumed to be binary (weak or strong).
source: In the cascade model, illustrated in Figure 2A, the degree of synaptic strength is still assumed to be binary (weak or strong); however, there are m states with different levels of plasticity α1, α2, …, αm, where α1>α2>…>αm.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the cascade model with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: In the cascade model, there are m states with different levels of plasticity α1, α2, …, αm, where α1>α2>…>αm.
source: In the cascade model, illustrated in Figure 2A, the degree of synaptic strength is still assumed to be binary (weak or strong); however, there are m states with different levels of plasticity α1, α2, …, αm, where α1>α2>…>αm.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the cascade model with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Entering less plastic states becomes less likely to occur with increasing depth in the cascade model.
source: Following (Fusi et al., 2005), we assume p1>p2>...>pm−1, meaning that entering less plastic states becomes less likely to occur with increasing depth.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption of the model following previous work.

claim: The cascade model of synapses can encode reward history on a wide, variable range of timescales.
source: We found that the cascade model of synapses can encode reward history on a wide, variable range of timescales.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work.

claim: The cascade model can consolidate the value information in a steady environment, as the synapses can become less plastic.
source: These features allow the model to consolidate the value information in a steady environment, as the synapses can become less plastic (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to simulation results in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The fluctuation of choice probability with the cascade model synapses becomes smaller as the model stays in the stable environment.
source: As seen in Figure 2C, the fluctuation of choice probability with the cascade model synapses becomes smaller as the model stays in the stable environment, where we artificially set that all synapses are initially at the most plastic states (top states).
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The cascade model fails to respond to a sudden, step-like change in the environment.
source: We also found, however, that this desirable property of memory consolidation also leads to a problem of resetting memory. In other words, the cascade model fails to respond to a sudden, step-like change in the environment (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to simulation results in Figure 2B,D.

claim: The time required to adapt to a new environment increases proportionally to the duration of the previous stable environment in the cascade model.
source: In fact, as seen in Figure 2D, the time required to adapt to a new environment increases proportionally to the duration of the previous stable environment.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Recent human experiments suggest that humans can react to sudden changes by increasing their learning rates.
source: Indeed, recent human experiments suggest that humans can react to such sudden changes by increasing their learning rates (Nassar et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: The surprise detection system compares the current difference in reward rates between a pair of timescales to the expected difference.
source: The main idea is to compare the reward information of multiple timescales that are stored in plastic (but not meta-plastic) synapses in order to detect changes on a trial-by-trial basis. More precisely, the system compares the current difference in reward rates between a pair of timescales to the expected difference; once the former significantly exceeds the latter, a surprise signal is sent to the decision making network to increase the rate of synaptic plasticity in the cascade models.
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism of the surprise detection system.

claim: When the unexpected uncertainty significantly exceeds the expected uncertainty, a surprise signal is sent to the decision making network.
source: More precisely, the system compares the current difference in reward rates between a pair of timescales to the expected difference; once the former significantly exceeds the latter, a surprise signal is sent to the decision making network to increase the rate of synaptic plasticity in the cascade models.
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism of the surprise detection system.

claim: The decision making network with cascade model synapses can now adapt to an unexpected change thanks to the surprise detection system.
source: Thanks to the surprise detection system, the decision making network with cascade model synapses can now adapt to an unexpected change. As seen in Figure 2C,D,F, it can successfully achieve both consolidation (i.e. accurate estimation of probabilities before the change point) and the quick adaptation to unpredicted changes in the environment.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to simulation results in Figure 2C,D,F.

claim: The model can successfully achieve both consolidation and quick adaptation to unpredicted changes in the environment.
source: As seen in Figure 2C,D,F, it can successfully achieve both consolidation (i.e. accurate estimation of probabilities before the change point) and the quick adaptation to unpredicted changes in the environment.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation results shown in Figure 2C,D,F.

claim: The distribution of synaptic plasticity decreases over time before the change point, but increases afterwards due to the surprise signal.
source: This can be seen prominently in Figure 2H, where the distribution of synaptic plasticity decreases over time before the change point, but increases afterwards due to the surprise signal.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation results shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Humans have a remarkable ability to change their learning rates depending on the volatility of their environment.
source: Experimental evidence shows that humans have a remarkable ability to change their learning rates depending on the volatility of their environment (Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The effective learning rate is on average significantly larger when the environment is rapidly changing than when the environment is more stable.
source: We found that the effective learning rate is on average significantly larger when the environment is rapidly changing (those trials in shorter blocks) than when the environment is more stable (those trials in longer blocks).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work.

claim: The learning rate was high in a smaller block (volatile) condition than in a larger block (stable) condition in experimental findings.
source: This is consistent with the experimental finding in (Behrens et al., 2007) that the learning rate was high in a smaller block (volatile) condition than in a larger block (stable) condition.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with citation.

claim: Within each block of trials, the learning rate is largest after the change point, decaying slowly over subsequent trials.
source: Also, within each block of trials, we found that the learning rate is largest after the change point, decaying slowly over subsequent trials.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work.

claim: The finding that learning rate is largest after the change point is consistent with both experimental findings and the predictions of optimal Bayesian models.
source: This is consistent with both experimental findings and the predictions of optimal Bayesian models (Nassar et al., 2010; Dayan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical work.

claim: The distribution of the rates of synaptic plasticity is dynamically self-tuned to a given environment in the model.
source: It should be noted that our model does not assume any a priori timescale of the environment. Rather, the distribution of the rates of synaptic plasticity is dynamically self-tuned to a given environment.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the model.

claim: The cascade model's effective learning rate is automatically tuned to the learning rate expected from the hand-tuned non-cascade plasticity model.
source: As can be seen, the cascade model's effective leaning rate is automatically tuned to the learning rate expected from the hand-tuned non-cascade plasticity model.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work.

claim: The agreement between cascade model and hand-tuned model is remarkable, as the cascade model did not assume any specific timescales nor any optimisation technique.
source: This agreement is remarkable, as we did not assume any specific timescales in our cascade model of plasticity nor any optimisation technique; rather, we assumed a wide range of timescales (1/αi's) and that synapses make reward-based plastic and metaplastic transitions by themselves, guided by surprise signals.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: The cascade model of metaplastic synapses can significantly outperform the model with fixed learning rates when the environment changes on multiple timescales.
source: Moreover, we found that our cascade model of metaplastic synapses can significantly outperform the model with fixed learning rates when the environment changes on multiple timescales, which is a very realistic situation but has yet to been explored experimentally.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work.

claim: The model of cascade synapses combined with surprise detection system can collect significantly more rewards than any model with fixed single synaptic plasticity.
source: As seen in Figure 3C, our model of cascade synapses combined with surprise detection system can collect significantly more rewards than any model with fixed single synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The synaptic plasticity distribution of the cascade model is self-tuned on a trial-by-trial basis, rather than on average over a long timescale.
source: This is because that the synaptic plasticity distribution of the cascade model is self-tuned on a trial-by-trial basis, rather than on average over a long timescale, as shown in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The model's performance is robust with a very wide range of threshold values for the surprise detection network.
source: We also found that this is true with a very wide range of threshold values for the surprise detection network, indicating that tuning of the threshold is not required.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work.

claim: The Bayesian model has been proposed to perform an optimal inference of changing reward probabilities and the volatility of the environment.
source: This Bayesian model has been proposed to perform an optimal inference of changing reward probabilities and the volatility of the environment.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the Bayesian model.

claim: Human behavioral data has been shown to be consistent with what the optimal Bayesian model predicted.
source: While human behavioral data has been shown to be consistent with what the optimal model predicted (Behrens et al., 2007), this model itself, however, does not account for how such an adaptive learning can be achieved neurally.
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: The Bayesian model does not account for how adaptive learning can be achieved neurally.
source: While human behavioral data has been shown to be consistent with what the optimal model predicted (Behrens et al., 2007), this model itself, however, does not account for how such an adaptive learning can be achieved neurally.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the Bayesian model.

claim: The neural model performed as well as the Bayesian learner model.
source: Remarkably, as seen in Figure 4, we found that our neural model (red) performed as well as the Bayesian learner model (black).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The reduction of fluctuations over trials in the neural model is strikingly similar to that the Bayesian model predicts.
source: Figure 4A contrasts the fluctuation of choice probability of our model to the Bayesian learner model under a fixed reward contingency. As seen, the reduction of fluctuations over trials in our model is strikingly similar to that the Bayesian model predicts.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The neural model performed as well as the Bayesian model across conditions in adaptation time, though marginally slower when the block was longer.
source: Figure 4B, on the other hand, shows the adaptation time as a function of the previous block size. Again, our model performed as well as the Bayesian model across conditions, though our model was marginally slower than the Bayesian model when the block was longer.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In experiments, pigeons showed a bias from the first session persistently over multiple sessions, most pertinently in the beginning of each session.
source: In these sessions, subjects showed a bias from the first session persistently over multiple sessions, most pertinently in the beginning of each session.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: The bias effect was modulated by the length of inter-session-intervals (ISIs) in experiments.
source: Crucially, this bias was modulated by the length of inter-session-intervals (ISIs).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: When birds had long ISIs, the bias effect was smaller and the adaptation was faster in experiments.
source: When birds had long ISIs, the bias effect was smaller and the adaptation was faster.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: The model can account for the spontaneous recovery of preference phenomenon.
source: We simulated our model in this experimental setting, and found that our model can account for this phenomenon (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The model shows a bias from the first session persistently over multiple sessions, most pertinently in the beginning of each session.
source: As seen in Figure 5, the model shows a bias from the first session persistently over multiple sessions (Sessions 2–4), most pertinently in the beginning of each session.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Learning was slower with shorter ISIs in the model, which is consistent with findings in Mazur (1996).
source: Also, learning was slower with shorter ISIs, which is consistent with findings in Mazur (1996).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work with citation to experimental study.

claim: The cascade model makes metaplastic transitions to deeper states during stable session 1, and those synapses are less likely to be modified in later sessions, remaining as a bias.
source: This is because the cascade model makes metaplastic transitions to deeper states (memory consolidation) during stable session 1, and those synapses are less likely to be modified in later sessions, remaining as a bias.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation of the modeling results.

claim: Synapses could be reset during each ISI due to forgetting transitions, the chance of which is higher with a longer ISI.
source: However, they could be reset during each ISI due to forgetting transitions (Figure 7), the chance of which is higher with a longer ISI.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation with reference to Figure 7.

claim: The surprise system played little role in spontaneous recovery, because forgetting during the ISI allowed many synapses to become plastic.
source: We also found that the surprise system played little role in this spontaneous recovery, because forgetting during the ISI allowed many synapses to become plastic, a function virtually similar to what the surprise system does at a block change in block-designed experiments.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling work.

claim: Not all synapses become plastic during the ISIs, leading to a persistent bias toward the previous preference.
source: Crucially, however, not all synapses become plastic during the ISIs, leading to a persistent bias toward the previous preference.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation of the modeling results.

claim: The model predicts that bias can develop over multiple sessions, and this is supported by experimental data.
source: Our model in fact predicts such a bias can develop over multiple sessions, and this is supported by experimental data (Iigaya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction with citation to experimental data.

claim: A relatively simple, well-studied decision-making network, when combined with a relatively simple model of synaptic plasticity guided by a surprise detection system, can capture a wide range of existing data.
source: While one might imagine that the circuits underlying such remarkable flexibility must be very complex, the current work suggests that a relatively simple, well-studied decision-making network, when combined with a relatively simple model of synaptic plasticity guided by a surprise detection system, can capture a wide range of existing data.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the work.

claim: Mackintosh proposed that learning should be enhanced if a stimulus predicts rewards.
source: The first was by Mackintosh (Mackintosh, 1975), in which he proposed that learning should be enhanced if a stimulus predicts rewards.
evidence: This is stated as a previous proposal with citation.

claim: Pearce and Hall proposed that learning rates should be increased when an outcome was unexpected.
source: The other influential proposal was made by Pearce and Hall (Pearce and Hall, 1980). They proposed that learning rates should be increased when an outcome was unexpected.
evidence: This is stated as a previous proposal with citation.

claim: The proposal that learning rates should be increased when an outcome was unexpected is at the heart of the model proposed in this work.
source: This indeed is at the heart of the model proposed here, where unexpected uncertainty enhanced synaptic plasticity and hence the learning rate.
evidence: This is stated as a connection between the current work and previous theory.

claim: The problem of change-point detection has long been studied in relation to the modulation of learning rates in reinforcement learning theory and Bayesian optimal learning theory.
source: In relation to surprise, the problem of change-point detection has long been studied in relation to the modulation of learning rates in reinforcement learning theory and Bayesian optimal learning theory (Pearce and Hall, 1980; Adams and MacKay, 2007; Dayan et al., 2000; Gallistel et al., 2001; Courville et al., 2006; Yu and Dayan, 2005; Behrens et al., 2007; Summerfield et al., 2011; Pearson and Platt, 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Previous models of change-point detection provided limited insight into how the algorithms can be implemented in neural circuits.
source: These models, however, provided limited insight into how the algorithms can be implemented in neural circuits.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous models.

claim: The model performs as well as a Bayesian learner model.
source: To fill this gap, we proposed a computation which is partially performed by bounded synapses, and we found that our model performs as well as a Bayesian learner model (Behrens et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with citation to the Bayesian model.

claim: The surprise detection algorithm was previously hinted by Aston-Jones and Cohen.
source: Nonetheless, the surprise detection algorithm that we propose was previously hinted by Aston and Cohen (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005), where they suggested that task-relevant values computed in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) are somehow integrated on multiple timescales and combined at the locus coeruleus (LC), as they proposed that the phasic and tonic release of norepinephrine (NE) controls the exploitation-exploration tradeoff.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: There is increasing evidence that the activity of ACC relates to the volatility of the environment or surprise signal.
source: In fact, there is increasing evidence that the activity of ACC relates to the volatility of the environment (Behrens et al., 2007) or surprise signal (Hayden et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The decision making network has three types of neural populations: an input population, action selection populations, and an inhibitory population.
source: The network has three types of neural populations: (1) an input population, which we assume to be uniformly active throughout each trial; (2) action selection populations, through which choices are made; and (3) an inhibitory population, through which different action selection populations compete.

claim: Choice corresponds to the winning action selection population, as determined by the synaptic strength projecting from input to action selection populations.
